enrichment.short_title: BASF refused early Norwich Pharmacal disclosure of pesticide supplier
key_facts: BASF AG sued ME2 Crop Protection for selling metazachlor under the name BOUNTY in alleged breach of BASF's patent.
ME2 initially claimed the imported product came from BASF or its associates and was legitimately on the market under EC exhaustion of rights.
ME2 later conceded the product was not from BASF or its licensees and appeared outside the Pesticide Safety Directorate marketing approval.
BASF sought disclosure of ME2's foreign supplier to enable possible proceedings abroad, while an interlocutory injunction already protected the UK market.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in patent infringement proceedings for Norwich Pharmacal-type disclosure of a foreign supplier.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused at this stage; disclosure deferred because the interlocutory injunction already protected BASF and ME2's non-infringement case might succeed at trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where an interlocutory injunction already protects the claimant's market and the defendant may succeed on non-infringement, it is inappropriate at that stage to order Norwich Pharmacal disclosure of the defendant's foreign supplier; the refusal is without prejudice to a further application if circumstances materially change.
legal_issues: Whether Norwich Pharmacal disclosure of a foreign supplier should be ordered before trial
Effect of an existing interlocutory injunction on the timing of disclosure relief
Whether possible success on non-infringement removes the basis for supplier disclosure

enrichment.short_title: Pharis deportation appeal refused; no automatic stay on filing notice
key_facts: Ben Pharis sought permission to appeal Maurice Kay J's refusal of judicial review of removal directions to Nigeria, claiming Sierra Leonean origin.
Maurice Kay J held removal was lawful because Nigeria was willing to receive him even if he was not a Nigerian national.
Pharis filed his notice of appeal out of time and was deported to Nigeria on 10 November 2003 after the Home Office failed to act on the Treasury Solicitor's deferral request.
The Home Office apologised after repeated court requests for an explanation of the administrative failure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal out of time against refusal of permission for judicial review in an immigration removal case.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the Court of Appeal announced that filing a notice of appeal in immigration judicial review cases will no longer automatically stay deportation unless a judge grants a stay on application.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 52.7 means an appeal does not automatically stay removal unless ordered; in immigration judicial review cases appellants must apply expressly for a stay, and unmeritorious appeals such as Pharis's would not have received one; deportation after filing a notice without a stay is not necessarily wrongful.
legal_issues: Whether removal directions to Nigeria were lawful under regulation 4 of the Immigration (Removal Directions) Regulations 2000
Whether Pharis's notice of appeal operated as a stay of deportation
Whether the Home Office acted unlawfully in deporting Pharis while an appeal was pending
Whether the Court of Appeal should change practice on automatic deferral of removal after filing a notice of appeal

enrichment.short_title: CPR 7.6(2) extension refused after solicitor's service delay
key_facts: Mr Hashtroodi suffered tetraplegia in a road traffic accident on 21 January 2000 and issued a claim form on 13 January 2001, eight days before limitation expired.
His solicitors failed to serve within four months and obtained a without-notice three-week extension from Master Tennant one working day before expiry.
Service on nominated solicitors via DX was probably lost; Deputy Master Eastman refused to set aside the extension and to strike out for non-service.
The Court of Appeal held the only reason for non-service was solicitor incompetence, not insurer delay in nominating solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by defendant against refusal to set aside a without-notice CPR 7.6 extension of time for service and against dismissal of a strike-out application.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Master Tennant's extension set aside; claimant to pay defendant's costs of the action and appeal.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 7.6(2) does not import the pre-CPR 'good reason' threshold from RSC Ord 6 r 8; the discretion must be exercised under the overriding objective, but failure to serve through solicitor incompetence after issuing at the last moment is a powerful reason to refuse an extension, especially where personal service on the defendant was readily available.

How the overriding objective governs extensions of time under CPR 7.6(2)
Whether a without-notice extension obtained by incompetent solicitors should be set aside
Whether service by DX under the former practice direction was effective (left undecided as moot)

enrichment.short_title: Terminally ill child's father not to be told by court order
key_facts: A four-year-old seriously ill child lived with his mother and stepfather under a residence order with a supervision order.
The father had no parental responsibility, a history of violence and drug offending, and had disclaimed interest in the child.
A circuit judge adjourned whether the local authority should tell the father of the child's terminal illness; Judge D ordered the authority to offer disclosure.
The mother appealed with Judge D's encouragement, arguing disclosure would risk violent disruption of the child's final weeks.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a specific issue order requiring a local authority to inform a non-resident father of his child's terminal medical condition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; paragraphs requiring the local authority to convey information to the father discharged; decision left to those with parental responsibility.
enrichment.ratio: Where no live dispute between parents falls to be decided, the court should not intervene under the non-interventionist Children Act 1989 to compel disclosure of a terminally ill child's condition to a violent father without parental responsibility; those with parental responsibility may decide not to inform him, and any Article 8 rights of the father are outweighed on the facts.
legal_issues: Whether the court had jurisdiction to order disclosure of a child's medical condition to the father
Whether a specific issue order was appropriate after discharge of the care order
Whether the local authority's supervision order role justified passing information to the father
Whether refusing disclosure breached the father's Article 8 ECHR rights

enrichment.short_title: Breckland farmland SSSI confirmation upheld against landowners
key_facts: Major Breckland landowners challenged English Nature's confirmation of about 13,335 hectares as a Site of Special Scientific Interest for an internationally important stone-curlew population.
English Nature notified the site in November 2000 and confirmed it in August 2001 after council approval in July 2001.
Lightman J dismissed the judicial review in July 2003, holding the confirmation lawful under section 28.
The appellants argued English Nature took account of immaterial considerations, misapplied section 28, and breached Article 1 Protocol 1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission on three grounds against dismissal of judicial review challenging confirmation of SSSI notification.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; confirmation lawful; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; appellants to pay respondent's costs.
enrichment.ratio: English Nature lawfully notified and confirmed Breckland Farmland as an SSSI under section 28 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 by directing its mind to the statutory criteria and guidelines independently of conflicting government policy; the decision was not vitiated by immaterial considerations, procedural irregularity, or disproportionate impact on the landowners' Article 1 Protocol 1 rights.

The correct construction of section 28 and the distinction between SSSI notification and SPA designation

enrichment.short_title: Video interview of Alzheimer's complainant admissible under section 23

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: The appellant Sed, a minicab driver, was convicted of attempted rape of an 81-year-old woman with moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease in a care home.
DNA matching the appellant was found on the complainant's knickers and an anal swab; he admitted consensual sexual contact but denied intercourse.
The prosecution relied on a video-recorded police interview of the complainant under sections 23 and 26 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
Psychiatrists agreed she was unfit to give live evidence and unreliable on detail but recalled an unpleasant sexual incident.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with renewed applications on hearsay admissibility, jury directions, and PACE Code C breach; sentence appeal also renewed.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed on all grounds; leave refused on remaining grounds including jury direction and second interview admissibility.
enrichment.ratio: Section 23 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 does not require common-law competence at the threshold; competence in the section 53 sense and reliability are matters for the section 26 interests-of-justice discretion, which the trial judge properly exercised in admitting the video interview of a vulnerable complainant whose account could be tested against medical and DNA evidence.
legal_issues: Whether competence is a precondition of admissibility under section 23
What test of competence applies to video-recorded hearsay under section 26
Whether admission of the complainant's interview was in the interests of justice and fair under section 78 and Article 6
Whether jury directions on the interview were adequate
Whether the second police interview breached Code C paragraph 11.4

enrichment.short_title: Barrister's negligent LRH Act advice damages assessed at £213,365

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993

key_facts: Trustee freeholders of Muswell Hill Broadway property sued solicitors and a barrister for negligence over leasehold enfranchisement notices served on tenant Mrs Tuttle.
The barrister admitted negligence in failing to advise that Mrs Tuttle's leases were not qualifying leases because each granted term was less than 21 years from the date of grant.
After a compromise treating Mrs Tuttle as entitled, the landlords granted long leases at premiums below open market value.
Only the barrister's admitted negligence on qualifying lease status was assessed; other allegations against both defendants were stayed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Assessment of damages on one admitted allegation of barrister's negligence after partial stay of professional negligence claims.
enrichment.outcome: Damages assessed at £213,365 plus interest at 6.5% from 18 July 2001; much of the claimed loss attributed to later compromise over invalid counter-notices was excluded under SAAMCO causation analysis.
enrichment.ratio: Loss flowing from compromise of proceedings over allegedly invalid counter-notices was not caused by negligent advice conceding qualifying lease status but by separate notice defects; damages for the admitted negligence must credit the premium an LVT would have fixed in July 2001 rather than the later compromise figure, and the block should be valued on an investment basis as at the date of the negligent act.
legal_issues: Whether loss from later compromise was caused by negligent advice on qualifying leases or by separate notice defects
Application of SAAMCO and The Oropesa to mitigation and causation
How to credit premiums and value the landlord's investment interest
Whether the property should be severed for loss assessment
The appropriate date for assessing damages

enrichment.short_title: Anti-suit injunction continued against New York arbitration petition
key_facts: Tonicstar, capital provider to Lloyd's Syndicate 1861, sued American Home Assurance in England for misrepresentation and non-disclosure over a facultative excess-of-loss reinsurance.
AHA discovered an arbitration clause after English proceedings were served and applied under section 9 for a stay while also petitioning the New York Federal Court to compel arbitration.
Gross J granted a without-notice anti-suit injunction restraining AHA's New York petition; this was the return date.
Both sides disputed the seat of arbitration and whether Tonicstar was a proper claimant, though the real party was the syndicate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Return date application to discharge or continue a without-notice anti-suit injunction restraining parallel New York proceedings to compel arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction continued until further order; England held the natural forum and AHA's New York petition oppressive.
enrichment.ratio: Where a Lloyd's reinsurance dispute governed by English law is already before the English court, including a section 9 stay application, pursuit of a New York petition to compel arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act is oppressive and warrants an anti-suit injunction to prevent pre-emption of the natural forum's decision on stay and seat.

Whether AHA's New York petition was vexatious or oppressive
Whether an anti-suit injunction should restrain parallel foreign arbitration compulsion proceedings

enrichment.short_title: Mental health judicial review permission refused for Miss Graham
key_facts: Miss Graham sought judicial review to prevent a mental health trust and social services authority from interfering with her liberty without court permission.
Staff had told her she would be sectioned under the Mental Health Act unless she agreed to medication for schizophrenia.
She was sectioned on 17 March 2004 and briefly detained at Homerton Hospital; habeas corpus proceedings ended when she was released.
Her grounds alleged persecution linked to the Russian Mafia and tenants at Follingham Court, Hackney.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Out-of-time application for permission to appeal Sullivan J's refusal of permission to apply for judicial review and interim relief.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; Sullivan J's decision upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Courts may in principle intervene to prevent unlawful detention, but without cogent evidence of an unlawful plan to deprive liberty the court cannot act on speculation; the Mental Health Act and habeas corpus provide remedies after detention, and the applicant's unsupported conspiracy-based grounds did not justify intervention.
